slides.title: Building the team on purpose
points: Hiring decides who joins, which shapes everything the team can do for years.
A good process is fair, consistent and predictive of the job.

slides.title: Define, structure, decide
points: Write down what the role needs before interviewing: skills, level, what success looks like at six months.
Structured interviews: each interviewer covers set areas with set questions and a scoring guide.
Work-like exercises predict better than puzzles.
Decide on evidence against the criteria, not on 'gut feel' or likeability.

slides.title: Speed against rigour
points: Slow processes lose good candidates; rushed ones hire mistakes.
Hiring for 'culture fit' can quietly mean hiring people like you; hire for values and what the team lacks.
Too many rounds exhaust candidates without improving decisions.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Interview training and calibration sessions.
Debriefs where each interviewer writes feedback before discussion.
A candidate experience survey.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Saying what we'll do, and roughly when
points: Planning chooses what the team works on; estimation gives a sense of size and time so others can plan too.
Estimates are forecasts with uncertainty, not promises.

slides.title: Slice, size, forecast
points: Break work into small, shippable slices; small things are easier to estimate and deliver.
Size relatively (this is bigger than that) rather than in exact hours.
Use past throughput to forecast: how many slices the team actually finishes per week.
Give ranges and confidence ('likely 4–6 weeks'), and update as you learn.

slides.title: Certainty is expensive
points: Detailed up-front plans go stale; rolling plans adapt.
Padding hides risk; naming risks is better.
Committing to scope, date and quality all at once rarely works; choose which flexes.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Quarterly goals with monthly check-ins.
Risks listed next to the plan.
Scope cut, not quality, when dates are fixed.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Keeping the people around the team aligned
points: Stakeholders are the people affected by or able to affect your team's work: product, other teams, leaders, customers.
Managing them is mostly communication and expectations.

slides.title: Know them, inform them, involve them
points: Map who cares about what, and how much influence they have.
Share progress and risks regularly, in their terms, before they ask.
Bring bad news early, with options.
Agree decisions and who makes them, in writing.

slides.title: Everyone can't get everything
points: Saying yes to everyone overloads the team; say no with reasons and alternatives.
Too many updates are noise; too few breed surprises.
Escalating is sometimes right; doing it without warning burns trust.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A short regular update: done, next, risks, asks.
Decision logs.
Roadmap conversations that start from goals, not feature lists.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Getting the right things finished
points: Execution is turning plans into shipped results, repeatedly, without burning out the team.
Most delivery problems are too much work in progress and unclear priorities.

slides.title: Focus, flow, feedback
points: Limit work in progress: finishing beats starting.
One clear priority order the whole team knows.
Remove blockers daily; that's much of a manager's job.
Measure flow (cycle time, throughput), not hours or busyness.

slides.title: Busy isn't productive
points: Starting many things at once makes everything late.
Process added to fix one slip often slows everything.
Heroics hide problems and burn people out.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A visible board with WIP limits.
Short check-ins focused on blockers.
Retrospectives that produce one or two real changes.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Helping people do their best work
points: Performance management sets expectations, gives feedback, supports growth, and deals with problems fairly.
Nothing in a review should be a surprise.

slides.title: Expectations, evidence, support
points: Clear expectations for each level (a career ladder) and each person's goals.
Regular feedback with examples, so reviews summarise rather than reveal.
Growth plans with real opportunities, not just advice.
Underperformance addressed early, with a specific plan, support and timeline.

slides.title: Kind isn't avoiding
points: Delaying hard conversations is unkind to the person and the team.
Ratings invite gaming; focus on impact and behaviour.
Bias creeps in; calibrate across managers and use evidence.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Calibration sessions across teams.
Written growth plans reviewed in one-to-ones.
Documented performance plans when needed.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: A team that works well together, sustainably
points: A healthy team shares information, disagrees openly, learns from mistakes and doesn't burn out.
Psychological safety, the belief that you can speak up without being punished, underlies it.

slides.title: Safety, clarity, sustainability
points: Make it safe to say 'I don't know', 'I made a mistake' and 'I disagree'.
Clear roles and goals reduce friction.
Watch for burnout signs: long hours, cynicism, withdrawal.
Run retrospectives and act on them.

slides.title: Comfort isn't the goal
points: Safe doesn't mean conflict-free; it means conflict about ideas is fine.
Surveys measure some things and miss others; talk to people.
Protecting the team sometimes means saying no upward.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Blameless postmortems.
A sustainable on-call rotation.
Managers who admit their own mistakes first.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: The manager's role when things break
points: During a serious incident, managers protect the responders, coordinate, and communicate upward and outward.
Afterwards, they make sure the lessons turn into change.

slides.title: Shield, support, follow up
points: Don't take over the technical response; support the incident commander.
Keep executives and customers informed so engineers can focus.
Watch for fatigue; rotate people on long incidents.
Make sure postmortem actions get time and owners.

slides.title: Presence without pressure
points: Hovering over responders slows them down.
Pushing for a cause before the fire is out costs time.
Promising 'never again' without investment rings hollow.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A communications lead role separate from the technical lead.
Food, breaks and handovers on long incidents.
Postmortem actions tracked in planning.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Choosing technical direction for the long term
points: Technical strategy decides where the systems should go over the next years and why: platforms, architecture, build or buy.
Good strategy is a few clear choices, explained.

slides.title: Diagnosis, policy, actions
points: Diagnose the real problem (slow delivery, outages, cost), with evidence.
Set guiding choices ('one way to run services', 'buy, don't build, for non-core needs').
Plan concrete steps, with milestones and owners.
Write it down and share it, so teams make consistent decisions.

slides.title: Choices mean saying no
points: A strategy that allows everything guides nothing.
Big rewrites rarely pay off; incremental migration usually wins.
Strategy without investment is a wish.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Architecture decision records.
Tech radar or standards documents.
Strategy reviewed yearly against what happened.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Developing the next leaders
points: As organisations grow, senior managers spend more time growing managers than managing engineers directly.
New managers need support; the job changes more than most expect.

slides.title: Transition, coaching, practice
points: The switch from engineer to manager changes how success is measured: through the team, not personal output.
Coach rather than solve: ask questions that help them find their answer.
Give them real responsibility with a safety net.
Peer groups and training help new managers learn from each other.

slides.title: Not everyone should manage
points: Promoting the best engineer into management can lose a great engineer and gain an unhappy manager.
A parallel senior engineering track keeps strong engineers growing.
Too much hand-holding slows their growth; too little sets them up to fail.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Manager onboarding plans.
Regular skip-level conversations.
Trial periods for engineers trying management.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: 'What would you do if…?' about people
points: Manager interviews ask about conflicts, low performance, a resignation, a burnt-out engineer.
They're scoring empathy, directness and judgement.

slides.title: Listen, clarify, act
points: Start by understanding: what's really happening, from each side.
Be direct about expectations and kind in how you say them.
Act with a plan and follow up.
Use real examples from your own experience.

slides.title: Neither soft nor harsh
points: Avoiding the issue fails the team; punishing first fails the person.
Fairness and consistency matter more than being liked.
Know when to involve HR.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Prepare stories: a conflict, a performance issue, a time you supported someone.
Practise the situation, actions, result structure.
Say what you learned.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: 'The project is slipping; what do you do?'
points: Execution questions test how you deliver: slipping projects, unclear priorities, dependencies on other teams.
They want concrete steps and trade-offs.

slides.title: Diagnose before fixing
points: Find the cause: scope growth, unclear requirements, technical debt, staffing, dependencies.
Options: cut scope, move dates, add focus (not just people), remove blockers.
Communicate the trade-off to stakeholders.
Learn from it for the next plan.

slides.title: Adding people isn't free
points: Adding engineers late often slows a project down at first.
Overtime fixes a week, not a quarter.
Hiding a slip makes it worse.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Have a real story of a project you rescued or a slip you managed.
Know a few delivery metrics.
Show how you communicated.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Thinking beyond the next sprint
points: Senior manager interviews include strategy: how you'd set direction, build a roadmap, or decide build versus buy.
They want structured thinking tied to business goals.

slides.title: Goals, options, choices
points: Start from the business goal and the current situation.
Lay out options with costs, risks and benefits.
Make a recommendation and say what you'd measure.
Explain how you'd bring the team and stakeholders along.

slides.title: Clarity over completeness
points: Listing every option without choosing doesn't show judgement.
Ignoring people and change management makes strategy fail.
Admit uncertainty and how you'd reduce it.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Prepare a story of a strategic decision you drove.
Practise build-versus-buy reasoning.
Know the company's business well enough to connect to it.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

newQuestions.stem: In a debrief, the first interviewer says 'strong hire', and everyone agrees. Some had doubts. What process prevents this?
choices: Each interviewer submits written feedback against the criteria before the debrief, then discusses evidence
Let the most senior person decide
why: Independent written feedback avoids anchoring and groupthink.

newQuestions.stem: A stakeholder asks for an exact delivery date for a large, unclear project. What's the most honest response?
choices: Give a range based on what's known, name the biggest unknowns, and commit to updating it as the first slices ship
Promise a date to keep them happy
Double your guess and say it's exact
why: Ranges with risks are honest and useful; updates keep trust.

newQuestions.stem: Your team will miss a date another team depends on. When should you tell them?
choices: As soon as you know, with the reason, the new estimate and options to reduce their impact
why: Early bad news lets them adapt; late news costs them.

newQuestions.stem: A team has 14 projects in progress for 6 engineers, and everything is late. What's the first lever?
choices: Cut work in progress: finish the top few before starting more
Start more projects to show progress
why: Fewer things at once means each finishes sooner.
Burns people out, doesn't fix flow.

newQuestions.stem: An engineer gets a 'below expectations' rating with no earlier feedback about it. What went wrong?
choices: Feedback wasn't given along the way; reviews should summarise known feedback, not surprise
why: Surprises in reviews mean feedback failed earlier.

newQuestions.stem: After a manager criticised an engineer publicly for an outage, people stopped reporting small mistakes. What's the fix?
choices: Rebuild safety: own the mistake publicly, move to blameless reviews, and thank people for raising problems
why: Speaking up returns when it's safe and valued.
Helps, but the culture problem remains.

newQuestions.stem: During a major outage, a director keeps joining the response channel asking engineers for updates every few minutes. What should the manager do?
choices: Set up a separate channel with regular updates from a comms lead, so responders can focus
Pause the response to brief them
why: Separating communication from response protects focus and keeps leaders informed.
Not necessary with a better channel.

newQuestions.stem: Teams use five different ways to deploy services, causing outages and slow onboarding. What's a strategic response?
choices: Choose one supported way, explain why, and plan an incremental migration with support for teams
why: A clear choice with a migration path reduces cost and risk.

newQuestions.stem: A new manager keeps doing the hardest technical work themselves and their team is stalling. How do you coach them?
choices: Help them see their impact now comes through the team: delegate the hard work with support, and spend their time unblocking and growing people
why: The core transition is from doing to enabling.

newQuestions.stem: Asked how you'd handle two senior engineers in open conflict about a design, what's a strong answer?
choices: Meet each to understand their views, then bring them together on the shared goal and decision criteria, and make sure a decision gets made and supported
Ignore it; seniors sort it out
Move one to another team immediately
why: Understanding, shared criteria and a clear decision resolve it fairly.

newQuestions.stem: A project is a month behind with six weeks left. The director suggests adding four engineers. What do you say?
choices: New people need onboarding and slow the team at first; look at cutting scope and removing blockers first, and add people only where work can split cleanly
Promise to catch up with overtime
why: Late additions often slow delivery; scope and focus are faster levers.

newQuestions.stem: Asked whether to build an internal tool or buy one, what's the strongest approach?
choices: Compare total cost, time to value, how core it is to the business, and risks; recommend one and say what would change your mind
why: Structured reasoning tied to the business shows judgement.
